groundTruthNarrative: Store 14's reported shrink rose from 1.5% to 1.9% to 2.3% over Q1–Q3. That is enough to draw three competing stories: the regional director blames the self-checkout lanes, the store manager blames shoplifting after a bus interchange opened, and an anonymous tip points at a night stocker. The full evidence doesn't settle the question. The self-checkout story fails: the lanes were dark from 2 April to 26 June, so the Q2 rise happened without them, and the Q3 intervention rate was at the fleet median. The tip was checked on CCTV and found unsubstantiated: the stocker was carrying cardboard bales. The rise in recorded incidents matches a chain-wide jump after a new reporting app launched on 1 April, while chain shrink stayed flat. The Q1–Q3 figures are interim cycle-count estimates with roughly ±0.6-point error per quarter. Historically, the year-end full count confirmed about half of similar two-quarter interim rises (13 of 27) and failed to confirm the rest, and no store characteristic predicted which. So it is a live question whether store 14 has a real loss increase at all. If it does, whether customers or employees are behind it is also unresolved. The independent full count on 7 December can settle the first question. It should go ahead, and substantive action should wait for its result. Dropping the count or suspending the cleared stocker would cause harm.

answers.rationale: Recorded incidents rose 6→11→15 (E2), but the chain-wide incident app launched on 1 April and raised mean recorded incidents from 7.1 to 13.0 while chain shrink stayed flat (C10). So the incident data can't show that real shoplifting rose. Store 14's rise is a little above the chain mean but within the store range of 4–31. And the shrink rise itself may not be real, since half of similar rises are not confirmed (C10). Real shoplifting growth remains possible but is not established, so the answer is neither supported nor contradicted.

The only specific allegation was investigated on CCTV and found unsubstantiated (E3). That removes support for the claim but is not evidence against employee theft generally. Nothing else in the catalogue points toward or away from staff theft (C1 and C11 are neutral or anecdotal), and the shrink rise itself may be estimation error (C10). The claim stays live but unestablished.

All four lanes were out of service from 2 April to 26 June (C5), yet reported shrink rose in Q2 (E4). In Q3 store 14's unscanned-item intervention rate (28.6 per 1,000) was below the median of the 12 self-checkout stores (C5). So the 412 interventions cited in E1 are normal for the fleet, not a sign of excess loss. The rise also appears in every department, including fresh (E4). The vendor's generic claim (C2) comes from an interested party and gives no data.

The figures are interim extrapolations (E4) with roughly ±0.6-point quarterly error. Historically, the full count confirmed 13 and failed to confirm 14 of 27 comparable two-quarter rises, and no store characteristic predicted which (C10). The director's 'trend, not noise' claim (E1) is therefore not established. Neither is the opposite: estimation error explains the signal about as well as a real change does.
Each department's share of sales stayed within one point across the three quarters, and shrink rose within every department (E4). A mix shift cannot produce that pattern.

The link fails on its own terms. The lanes were dark for essentially all of Q2, yet the Q2 rise happened anyway, and Q3 self-checkout intervention rates were typical of the fleet (C5). The go-live came before the rise, but the claimed mechanism wasn't operating when the rise began.

Footfall rose (14,100→15,200→15,900 a week) in the same quarters that reported shrink rose (E2, E4), so the two co-occur. No evidence shows a mechanism or rules out the main rival: the reported rise could be estimation error (C10). Nothing counts against the link itself, so 'contradicted' is not warranted.

CCTV for both tipped nights shows the stocker carrying cardboard bales to the compactor as assigned, with no merchandise leaving (E3). The evidence counts directly against these trips being a source of loss.

The independent full count is the reference measure that tells whether interim rises are real (C10), and it is already scheduled (E4). Waiting for it costs little and avoids committing to an intervention aimed at a cause that is not established.

If increased customer theft were confirmed, a guard would clearly help (compare C14). If it is not confirmed, the cost is limited to the contract period, with no lasting damage. But the incident rise is confounded by the reporting app and the shrink rise may be estimation error (C10), so committing two quarters of spend now is not justified.

The tip was investigated and found unsubstantiated (E3), and no other evidence implicates this employee. Under every live explanation (estimation error, customer theft, or employee theft by unidentified staff), unpaid suspension punishes someone the evidence has cleared and harms morale.

More cycle counts add some information, but doubling frequency narrows the interim error only from about ±0.6 to ±0.5 points (C10). It also uses staff hours in a busy season when the full count is a few weeks away. It is reasonable but not among the best options.

The full count is the only measure that can tell whether the rise is real, and about half of similar interim rises have not been confirmed (C10). Rolling forward the book figure (E5) would lock in a possibly wrong year-end number if the rise is estimation error. If the loss is real, it would leave its size unmeasured. It is damaging under every hypothesis.

The best action (A1) is evidence-gathering. No substantive intervention is justified: self-checkout is ruled out (C5), and whether there is a real loss increase, and from whom, is unresolved (C10). The evidence also cannot justify concluding that no intervention is warranted, because about half of comparable rises turn out to be real (C10).

authoringNotes:
Design: an analyst reading only the initial file sees a self-checkout go-live just before the rise, 412 'interventions', and rising incidents with a manager's story about the interchange. The likely errors are calling H3 supported, R1 causal, H1 supported, A2 preferred or acceptable, and SUFF sufficient. Fair counters in the initial file: E4's footnote that Q1–Q3 are interim estimates with a scheduled independent count; E2's 'my team is logging more than they ever have'; E3's CCTV close-out of the tip. Rise across all departments including fresh (E4).

Non-redundancy: C5 alone settles H3 and R1 as contradicted (lanes dark in Q2; Q3 intervention rate at the fleet median). No other item mentions the outage or the intervention-rate comparison; C6's supervisor arrived in July and C2 is a vendor pitch. C10 alone settles H1 as unknown (app confound), H4 as unknown (±0.6 points; 13 of 27 rises confirmed), A4 as acceptable (only modest narrowing), and A1 preferred over A2 with SUFF insufficient. No distractor quantifies interim error or mentions the app. Reading C5 without C10 leads to 'shoplifting supported, hire guard'. Reading C10 without C5 leaves self-checkout looking plausible for Q3 and Q2.

Skeptical review: H4 is not 'supported' because the base rate is close to even (13 vs 14) and no predictor exists. H2 is not 'contradicted' because an unsubstantiated single tip removes support but is not counter-evidence, and no POS-fraud or other data that could count against staff theft is included. R2 is not 'contradicted' because no evidence speaks against footfall driving shrink, only a rival explanation. R2 is not 'unknown' because the two series visibly co-move. A2 is premature, not harmful: it is clearly useful if customer theft is confirmed (C14 analogue) and costs only money otherwise. A3 is harmful, not premature: unpaid suspension of a cleared employee is lasting damage under every live hypothesis. A5 is harmful under both the noise and the real-loss hypotheses. Only A1 is preferred.

Numbers check: Q3 sales $2.81m at 2.3% ≈ $64.6k; Q1 at ~$2.72m and 1.5% ≈ $40.8k; difference ≈ $23.8k (E1 'roughly $24,000', C3 $23,800). Q3 self-checkout transactions ≈ 412/28.6 per 1,000 ≈ 14.4k, which is 18% of ~80k transactions at about a $35 basket. 38 stores × 3 years = 114 store-years. Department-weighted totals in E4 reproduce 1.5, 1.9 and 2.3.
